subject: science
name: Carbon and its Compounds
summary: Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons. Because of catenation and tetravalency it forms a huge number of compounds — saturated and unsaturated, chains and rings — grouped into homologous series and named by IUPAC rules. Carbon compounds undergo combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are two important carbon compounds, and soaps and detergents clean by forming micelles.

topics.title: Bonding in carbon: the covalent bond
topics.summary: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and forms bonds by sharing electrons (covalent bonds) — single, double or triple.
topics.simple: Carbon has 4 electrons in its outer shell. It can't easily lose or gain 4 electrons, so it **shares** electrons with other atoms. A bond made by sharing a pair of electrons is a **covalent bond**.
topics.explain:
Carbon (atomic number 6) has the configuration **2, 4**. To reach a noble-gas arrangement it would have to:
- gain 4 electrons → C⁴⁻: hard, because 6 protons can't easily hold 10 electrons
- lose 4 electrons → C⁴⁺: needs too much energy, as only 2 electrons would be held by 6 protons

So carbon **shares** its valence electrons. A bond formed by sharing a pair of electrons between two atoms is a **covalent bond**.

**Examples (electron-dot structures):**
- **H₂:** single bond, H–H
- **O₂:** double bond (2 shared pairs), O=O
- **N₂:** triple bond (3 shared pairs), N≡N
- **CH₄ (methane):** carbon shares one electron pair with each of 4 hydrogen atoms
- **H₂O, NH₃** also have covalent bonds

**Properties of covalent compounds:**
- generally **low melting and boiling points** (weak forces between molecules)
- generally **poor conductors** of electricity — no ions are formed

This contrasts with ionic compounds, which have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved.
topics.deep: Methane is used as a fuel and is a major part of biogas and CNG (compressed natural gas).
topics.example: The LPG and CNG used in homes and autos in India are mainly carbon compounds — butane and methane — held together by covalent bonds. That's why they are gases with very low boiling points.
keyPoints: Carbon: 2, 4 → 4 valence electrons
Carbon shares electrons instead of forming C⁴⁺ or C⁴⁻
Covalent bond = sharing of an electron pair
Single (H₂), double (O₂), triple (N₂) bonds
Covalent compounds: low melting/boiling points, poor conductors
Methane CH₄: carbon bonded to 4 H atoms

topics.title: Versatile nature of carbon; allotropes; hydrocarbons
topics.summary: Catenation and tetravalency let carbon form chains, branches and rings. Hydrocarbons can be saturated (alkanes) or unsaturated (alkenes, alkynes). Diamond, graphite and fullerenes are allotropes of carbon.
topics.simple: Carbon atoms can join to each other to make long chains, branched chains and rings — this is **catenation**. Each carbon can make 4 bonds (**tetravalency**). Together, these let carbon form millions of compounds. Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen are **hydrocarbons**.
topics.explain:
**Allotropes of carbon** — different forms of the same element:
- **Diamond:** each carbon is bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D structure; hardest natural substance, does not conduct.
- **Graphite:** each carbon is bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; one double bond per carbon satisfies its valency; layers slide over each other, so it is smooth and slippery; a good conductor.
- **Fullerenes:** C-60, shaped like a football (named buckminsterfullerene).

**Why so many carbon compounds?**
1. **Catenation** — carbon links with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings. C–C bonds are very strong and stable.
2. **Tetravalency** — carbon bonds with 4 other atoms (H, O, N, S, Cl, etc.). Its small size lets the nucleus hold the shared electrons strongly, so bonds are strong.

**Hydrocarbons:**
- **Saturated** (only single bonds) — **alkanes**, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈
- **Unsaturated** (double or triple bonds) — **alkenes** CₙH₂ₙ (ethene C₂H₄, one C=C) and **alkynes** CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne C₂H₂, one C≡C)

Carbon compounds can be **straight chains**, **branched chains** or **rings**. Butane C₄H₁₀ has two forms — a straight chain and a branched chain — with the same formula but different structures; these are **structural isomers**. **Cyclohexane** C₆H₁₂ is a saturated ring; **benzene** C₆H₆ is a ring with alternating double bonds.
topics.example: The 'lead' in your pencil is actually graphite — its soft layers slide off onto paper. The diamond in a ring and the graphite in a pencil are both pure carbon; only the arrangement of atoms differs.
keyPoints: Allotropes: diamond (hard), graphite (conducts), fullerene C-60
Catenation: carbon bonds with carbon to form chains and rings
Tetravalency: carbon forms 4 bonds
Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (single bonds) are saturated
Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ and alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ are unsaturated
Structural isomers: same formula, different structure (butane)
Benzene C₆H₆ and cyclohexane C₆H₁₂ are rings

topics.title: Functional groups, homologous series and nomenclature
topics.summary: A functional group gives a compound its characteristic properties. Compounds with the same functional group differing by –CH₂– form a homologous series. IUPAC names use a root for the carbon count plus a suffix/prefix for the functional group.
topics.simple: Some atoms or groups (like –OH or –COOH) decide how a carbon compound behaves — these are **functional groups**. A family of compounds with the same functional group where each member has one extra –CH₂– is a **homologous series**. Names are built from the number of carbons plus an ending for the group.
topics.explain:
An atom other than C and H in a carbon compound is a **heteroatom** (O, N, Cl, etc.). A heteroatom or group of atoms that gives the compound its specific properties is a **functional group**:
- **Halo** (–Cl, –Br): chloromethane, CH₃Cl
- **Alcohol** (–OH): ethanol, C₂H₅OH
- **Aldehyde** (–CHO): ethanal, CH₃CHO
- **Ketone** (>C=O): propanone, CH₃COCH₃
- **Carboxylic acid** (–COOH): ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH

**Homologous series:** a series of compounds with the **same functional group** and similar chemical properties, where successive members differ by **–CH₂–** (14 u in mass). Example: CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH. As molecular mass increases, physical properties like melting point, boiling point and solubility change **gradually**, but chemical properties stay similar.

**Naming (IUPAC) — steps:**
1. Count the carbon atoms → root: 1 meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex.
2. Identify the functional group and add the right suffix or prefix:
- alkane: -ane; alkene: -ene; alkyne: -yne
- alcohol: -ol (drop final 'e': propane → propanol)
- aldehyde: -al; ketone: -one; carboxylic acid: -oic acid
- halogen: prefix chloro-/bromo- (chloropropane)

Worked example: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → 3 carbons (prop), –OH group → **propanol**. CH₃CH₂COOH → 3 carbons, –COOH → **propanoic acid**. CH₃CH₂CHO → **propanal**.
topics.example: Methanol (CH₃OH), ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and propanol (C₃H₇OH) are neighbours in the alcohol homologous series. Each has one more –CH₂– unit (14 u heavier) than the previous one, and all react with sodium to give hydrogen.
keyPoints: Functional group decides chemical properties
Alcohol –OH, aldehyde –CHO, ketone >C=O, acid –COOH, halo –Cl/–Br
Homologous series: same functional group, differ by –CH₂– (14 u)
Physical properties change gradually; chemical properties similar
Roots: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6
Suffixes: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -ene, -yne

topics.title: Chemical properties of carbon compounds
topics.summary: Carbon compounds burn (combustion), can be oxidised to acids, unsaturated ones add hydrogen (hydrogenation), and saturated ones undergo substitution with chlorine in sunlight.
topics.simple: Carbon compounds burn in air to give CO₂, water, heat and light. Alcohols can be oxidised to acids. Unsaturated compounds can add hydrogen across their double bond. Saturated compounds can swap their hydrogen for chlorine in sunlight.
topics.explain:
**1. Combustion:** carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give CO₂, water, heat and light.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat and light
- **Saturated** hydrocarbons usually burn with a clean **blue flame**.
- **Unsaturated** hydrocarbons burn with a **yellow, sooty flame**.
In a limited supply of air, even saturated fuels give a sooty flame. If the bottom of your cooking vessel blackens, the air holes of the stove are blocked and fuel is being wasted. Coal and petroleum contain nitrogen and sulphur, so burning them releases oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, which pollute the air. A flame is produced only when gaseous substances burn; charcoal just glows.

**2. Oxidation:** alcohols are converted to carboxylic acids by **oxidising agents** such as **alkaline potassium permanganate** (KMnO₄) or acidified potassium dichromate.
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH (with alkaline KMnO₄ + heat)
The pink colour of KMnO₄ disappears as it is used up.

**3. Addition reaction:** unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst such as **nickel** or palladium to give saturated hydrocarbons. This **hydrogenation** is used to make **vanaspati ghee** from vegetable oils.
RCH=CHR + H₂ → RCH₂CH₂R (Ni catalyst)
Animal fats contain saturated fatty acids, which are said to be harmful to health; oils with unsaturated fatty acids should be chosen for cooking.

**4. Substitution reaction:** saturated hydrocarbons are quite unreactive, but in **sunlight**, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one:
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (in sunlight)
topics.example: When the gas stove gives a yellow flame and blackens the kadhai, the air holes are clogged and combustion is incomplete. Cleaning the burner restores the blue flame and saves gas.
keyPoints: Combustion: carbon compound + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + heat + light
Saturated: blue flame; unsaturated: yellow sooty flame
Oxidation: ethanol → ethanoic acid (alkaline KMnO₄)
Addition (hydrogenation) with Ni catalyst makes vanaspati
Substitution: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in sunlight
A catalyst changes reaction rate without being used up

topics.title: Ethanol and ethanoic acid
topics.summary: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a liquid used in medicines and as a fuel; ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH, acetic acid) is the acid in vinegar. Together they form a sweet-smelling ester.
topics.simple: **Ethanol** is the alcohol used in tinctures, cough syrups and as a fuel. **Ethanoic acid** is the acid in vinegar. When the two react with a little sulphuric acid, they make a sweet-smelling compound called an **ester**.
topics.explain:
**Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)**
- Liquid at room temperature, soluble in water.
- Used in tincture of iodine, cough syrups and tonics; in alcoholic drinks. Even small amounts of pure ethanol (absolute alcohol) are dangerous, and drinking it slows metabolism and depresses the nervous system.
- Industrial alcohol is made unfit to drink by adding poisonous **methanol** and a blue dye; this is **denatured alcohol**. Methanol can cause blindness and death.
- **Reaction with sodium:** 2Na + 2CH₃CH₂OH → 2CH₃CH₂O⁻Na⁺ (sodium ethoxide) + H₂
- **Dehydration:** heated at 443 K with excess **concentrated sulphuric acid**, ethanol loses water to give **ethene**: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
- Ethanol from sugarcane can be mixed with petrol as a cleaner fuel.

**Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH)** — also called acetic acid
- **Vinegar** is a 5–8% solution of ethanoic acid in water, used as a preservative in pickles.
- Pure ethanoic acid freezes in cold climates (melting point 290 K), so it's called **glacial acetic acid**.
- It is a **weak acid** (unlike HCl, a strong mineral acid).
- **Esterification:** CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ (ethyl ethanoate, an ester) + H₂O, in the presence of an acid catalyst. Esters smell sweet and are used in perfumes and flavours.
- **Saponification:** an ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt of the acid. This reaction is used to make soap.
- **With a base:** NaOH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa (sodium ethanoate/sodium acetate) + H₂O
- **With carbonates and hydrogencarbonates:** 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂; CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂
topics.example: Achaar makers add vinegar to pickles. Its ethanoic acid keeps the pickle acidic so that microbes can't grow, which helps it last for months.
keyPoints: Ethanol C₂H₅OH: used in medicines, as a fuel; denatured with methanol
Ethanol + Na → sodium ethoxide + H₂
Ethanol + hot conc. H₂SO₄ (443 K) → ethene + water
Vinegar = 5–8% ethanoic acid; pure form = glacial acetic acid
Acid + alcohol → ester (sweet smell): esterification
Ester + NaOH → alcohol + salt: saponification
Ethanoic acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂

topics.title: Soaps and detergents
topics.summary: Soap molecules have a water-loving ionic end and an oil-loving carbon chain; they form micelles that trap oily dirt. Detergents work even in hard water.
topics.simple: A soap molecule is like a tadpole: the head loves water and the long tail loves oil. In water, the tails grab oily dirt and the heads face outward, forming a ball called a **micelle**. Rinsing washes the micelles away. Soap doesn't lather well in hard water, but detergents do.
topics.explain:
**Soaps** are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (made by saponification of fats/oils).

A soap molecule has two ends:
- an **ionic (hydrophilic) end** — the –COO⁻Na⁺ part, which dissolves in water
- a long **hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) chain**, which dissolves in oil

**How soap cleans — micelles:** in water, soap molecules arrange themselves so the hydrocarbon tails point inward (towards the oily dirt) and the ionic heads point outward (towards the water). This cluster is a **micelle**. Oily dirt is collected in the centre of the micelle. The micelles stay suspended in water as a colloid and don't come together, because their ionic surfaces repel each other. Rinsing with water removes the dirt. A soap solution looks cloudy because micelles scatter light.

**Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble precipitate called **scum**, so a lot of soap is wasted and lather forms poorly.

**Detergents** are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions; they have long hydrocarbon chains too. Their charged ends **don't form insoluble precipitates** with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work well even in **hard water**. They are used in shampoos and products for cleaning clothes.
topics.example: Bathing with soap in a hostel that gets borewell (hard) water leaves a sticky white layer in the bucket — that's scum. Washing powders (detergents) don't form this scum, so they clean well even in hard water.
keyPoints: Soap = Na/K salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid
Ionic head: hydrophilic; hydrocarbon tail: hydrophobic
Micelle: tails inward around the dirt, heads outward
Hard water (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) forms scum with soap
Detergents work in hard water
Saponification makes soap

faqs.q: Why does carbon form covalent bonds and not ionic bonds?
faqs.a: Carbon has 4 valence electrons. Gaining 4 electrons (C⁴⁻) is hard because 6 protons can't hold 10 electrons, and losing 4 (C⁴⁺) needs a lot of energy. So carbon shares its electrons with other atoms and forms covalent bonds.

faqs.q: What is the difference between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons?
faqs.a: **Saturated** hydrocarbons (alkanes) have only single C–C bonds, e.g. ethane C₂H₆; they burn with a blue flame and undergo substitution. **Unsaturated** hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, e.g. ethene C₂H₄ or ethyne C₂H₂; they burn with a sooty flame and undergo addition reactions.

faqs.q: How does soap remove oily dirt?
faqs.a: A soap molecule has a water-loving ionic end and an oil-loving hydrocarbon tail. In water, the tails dig into the oily dirt and the heads stay in the water, forming micelles with the dirt trapped inside. Rinsing with water carries the micelles, and the dirt, away.

faqs.q: Why don't soaps work well in hard water?
faqs.a: Hard water has calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble, sticky precipitate called scum, so a lot of soap is wasted and little lather forms. Detergents don't form such precipitates, so they work in hard water.

faqs.q: What is the difference between esterification and saponification?
faqs.a: **Esterification** is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol (acid catalyst) to form an ester and water. **Saponification** is the reverse type of process: an ester reacts with sodium hydroxide to give back an alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid. Saponification is used to make soap.

Ethanol meant for industrial use is made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous methanol and a blue dye so that it can be identified easily. This is called denatured alcohol. Methanol can cause blindness and even death.

quiz.q: The number of valence electrons in a carbon atom is:
quiz.explain: Carbon is 2, 4 — it has 4 electrons in its outer shell.

quiz.q: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in a nitrogen (N₂) molecule?
quiz.explain: N₂ has a triple bond, N≡N, i.e. three shared electron pairs.

quiz.q: Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity?
quiz.explain: Graphite conducts electricity; diamond does not.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
quiz.explain: Ethene C₂H₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ and has a C=C double bond. The others are alkanes.

quiz.q: The property of carbon to form long chains by bonding with other carbon atoms is called:
quiz.explain: Catenation is self-linking of carbon atoms.

quiz.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CHO is:
Successive members of a homologous series differ in molecular mass by:
quiz.explain: They differ by –CH₂–, which is 12 + 2 × 1 = 14 u.

quiz.q: Conversion of vegetable oil into vanaspati ghee is an example of:
quiz.explain: Hydrogen is added to the unsaturated oil using a nickel catalyst.

quiz.q: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in sunlight is a:
quiz.explain: A chlorine atom replaces a hydrogen atom of methane.

quiz.q: Ethanol heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K gives:
quiz.explain: Conc. H₂SO₄ removes water (dehydration): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.

quiz.q: The sweet-smelling compound formed when ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol is:
In a micelle, the hydrocarbon tails of soap molecules point:
quiz.explain: Hydrophobic tails attach to the oil at the centre; ionic heads face the water.
